Renart is the fast visual workspace for Bruin projects.

It is designed for people who want to inspect, edit, and run pipelines quickly while keeping the underlying project in version-controlled files.

## Good fit for

- Data engineers building pipelines
- Analytics engineers working in SQL-heavy projects
- Technical data users who want a more visual workflow around Bruin projects

## What Renart helps with

- Seeing assets, dependencies, lineage, and data flow on a canvas
- Editing pipelines faster than working only through YAML and SQL files
- Running inspect and materialization flows from the same workspace view
- Staying close to real project files that work well with Git

When to use Bruin CLI and when to use Renart.

Bruin CLI and Renart work on the same projects, but they support different working styles.

## Bruin CLI

Bruin CLI is a better fit when you want a more coding-oriented, terminal-first experience.

Typical cases:

- editing files directly in your editor
- running commands from the terminal
- working in a script-heavy or automation-heavy loop

## Renart

Renart is a better fit when you want a faster visual workflow.

Typical cases:

- exploring a pipeline on a canvas
- understanding dependencies and lineage quickly
- editing assets with more context around them
- inspecting and running work without leaving the workspace view

## Same project model

Both work against the same underlying project files. Renart is not a separate project format.

Install Renart with:

```bash
curl -LsSf getrenart.com/install.sh | sh
```

The installer downloads the matching release binary from GitHub Releases and places it in your local bin directory.

The repository keeps the checked-in installer generated from:

```bash
PATH="$HOME/go/bin:$PATH" binst init --source=goreleaser --file=.goreleaser.yaml -o .config/binstaller.yml
PATH="$HOME/go/bin:$PATH" binst gen --config=.config/binstaller.yml -o install.sh
```

## Current local setup

If you are working from the repository directly, you can still run Renart with:

```bash
go run . web
```

## Important

Start Renart inside a Git repository.

Renart is designed around Git-backed project workspaces, and some workspace flows expect that repository context to exist.
Create and run a local DuckDB sample pipeline in Renart.

The fastest way to try Renart is the DuckDB quickstart. It creates the Bruin chess sample project in your current Git workspace, adds local DuckDB and chess connections, and materializes the sample pipeline from the Renart onboarding flow.

## Start Renart

Open Renart from an empty Git-backed workspace:

```bash
renart web
```

If the workspace has no pipelines or connections yet, Renart opens onboarding automatically.

## Choose The Quickstart

On the welcome screen, click **Create playground** in the quickstart card. Renart creates and runs the sample, then opens the workspace canvas directly.

![Renart onboarding quickstart card with a chess DAG preview](/quickstart-onboarding.png)

## Explore The Pipeline

Use the canvas tour to inspect the sample data flow:

![Renart quickstart workspace canvas with chess assets](/quickstart-workspace.png)

- `quickstart.players` is an ingestr asset that loads chess player profiles into DuckDB.
- `quickstart.games` is an ingestr asset that loads chess games into DuckDB.
- `quickstart.player_stats` is a SQL asset that joins players to games and aggregates player counts.
- `quickstart.my_python_asset` is a tiny Python asset included in the Bruin default template.

The pipeline has already been materialized, so the DuckDB database contains the sample tables.

## Next Steps

Use the quickstart as a safe local playground:

- edit the SQL assets and watch Renart save the underlying files
- materialize the pipeline again from the workspace
- create a downstream asset from the canvas
- replace the sample SQL with your own DuckDB queries

If you already have warehouse tables, go back through onboarding and choose **Import an existing warehouse** instead.
Start Renart and open a workspace.

## Start Renart

From `renart/`:

```bash
go run . web
```

If you want to point Renart at a specific Bruin binary:

```bash
go run . web --bruin-binary /path/to/bruin
```

## Local validation flow

```bash
go build .
cd web
corepack pnpm test:e2e:live
```

## Workspace model

Renart works directly against the files in your project workspace. Changes made through the UI are meant to stay compatible with a Git-based workflow.
